the Bear Island and Sftorfjorden submarine fans were fed by large volumes of glacial debris, and that the sedimentation rates over these fans were high enough to account for the volumes of late glacial sediment inferred from seismic data.
the Bear Island and the Storfjord fans have a similar depositional history, and the ice-sheet model provides a reasonable estimate of the timing of glaciation of the Arctic High-Latitude region.

the late Weichelsian Eurasian ice sheet had a maximum thickness of about 1400–1600 m over the Barent Sea shelf, and that ice-streams within bathymetrically confined troughs transported about 4000 km 2 and 700 km 3 sediment to the Bear Island and the Storfjordon trough mouths, respectively, between 28 and 12 ka.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the numerical ice-sheet model is a valuable tool in the study of glacial sedimentation on the Arctic continental margins.
ice-sheet modeling, in conjunction with geophysical and sedimentological data, can provide a quantitative framework for the interpretation of glacially-derived sedimentation on continental margins.
the ice-sheet model results are consistent with the geophysical measurements of sedimentation on the Barents and Kara Sea margins.
The main takeaway from our work is that
ice-sheet numerical modeling and geophysical measurements can be combined to reconstruct glacial history and sediment transport on the Arctic shelf.
the numerical ice-sheet model is capable of producing the correct magnitude of sedimentation at the continental margin, and the timing of sediment delivery to the continental shelf.
